simulator.title: Break it on purpose
simulator.sub: Fire an attack and watch which check stops it, why, and how to fix it. Every finding here is real output from the tools in this template.
simulator.note: The first four gates run on your laptop at every commit. Tests and the dependency scan run in CI, on GitHub.

attacks.why: gitleaks found a GitHub token (rule github-pat) in src/app/client.py, line 1. The commit stopped on your laptop, so the token never reached GitHub.
attacks.fix: Read the token from an environment variable, name the variable in .env.example, and commit again.

attacks.why: ruff S608: Possible SQL injection vector through string-based query construction. The name goes straight into the query text.
attacks.fix: Pass values as parameters: db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,)).

attacks.why: ShellCheck SC2086: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. A file name with a space or a * in it would delete the wrong files.
zizmor unpinned-uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.33.1 is not pinned to a hash. On 19 March 2026 attackers moved 76 of that action's 77 tags to code that stole CI secrets (CVE-2026-33634).
attacks.fix: Pin the full 40-character commit SHA with a # vX.Y.Z comment. Dependabot keeps it current.

attacks.why: zizmor template-injection: github.event.issue.title is pasted into a run script, so anyone who opens an issue can run commands in your CI.
attacks.fix: Pass it in through env (TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}) and use "$TITLE" in the script.

attacks.why: pytest: test_rejects_garbage failed with DID NOT RAISE ValueError. A string shortcut stopped checking that the input is an address at all.
attacks.fix: Restore the real parsing with the ipaddress module, run make test, then push again.

attacks.why: Trivy found 8 high-severity CVEs in urllib3 1.26.4 in uv.lock, from CVE-2021-33503 to CVE-2026-97689.
attacks.fix: Bump urllib3 to 2.8.0 or newer, run uv lock, then push again.

attacks.why: Every gate passed: no secrets, no risky code, pinned workflows, green tests, no known-vulnerable libraries.
attacks.fix: Nothing to fix. Open the pull request and ask for a review.

cards.title: Secrets stop on your laptop

stages.title: Get your copy
stages.summary: Make your own repository from the template, then open it where you'll work.

steps.title: Create your repository from the template
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: A template copies every file into a new repository that starts with a single commit, so your project begins clean and nobody else's history comes with it.

do.text: On GitHub, open the template and press Use this template, then Create a new repository.
Pick a name and choose Public or Private (see the note below), then press Create repository.

check.text: Your new repository shows the same files and one first commit.

undo.text: Settings › General › Danger Zone › Delete this repository. Only for a repository you just made: it can't be undone.

callouts.label: Public or private
callouts.text: On GitHub Free, a private repository can't publish GitHub Pages, can't enforce branch rules, and doesn't get dependency review. Choose Public unless the code must stay hidden.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Creating a repository from a template

steps.title: Open it in Codespaces, no install needed
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: A codespace is a computer in the cloud with every tool already installed by the dev container. It's the fastest way to start, on any laptop.

do.text: On your repository page press Code › Codespaces › Create codespace on main. While it builds, the dev container runs `make setup` for you.
When the editor opens, run this in its terminal:

check.text: You see the list of make targets. `ls .git/hooks/pre-commit` prints the path, so the checks will run on every commit.

undo.text: Code › Codespaces › the ⋯ menu › Delete. Commit and push first: anything not pushed is lost with the codespace.

callouts.label: Free plan
callouts.text: GitHub Free includes 120 core hours and 15 GB of Codespaces storage a month. Stop the codespace when you're done so it doesn't use them up.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: About billing for GitHub Codespaces

steps.title: Or copy it to your own computer
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: Working locally is faster day to day. You need git, make, Python 3.12 or newer, and uv, the tool that installs the exact versions this project locks.

do.text: Install uv with your system's package manager:
Then copy the repository. Replace YOUR-USER and YOUR-REPO with yours:

check.text: `git status` says you're on branch main with nothing to commit.

replay.out: Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
nothing to commit, working tree clean

undo.text: Delete the folder. Nothing on GitHub changes.

callouts.label: Windows
callouts.text: The Makefile needs bash. On Windows, work inside WSL or use Codespaces.

stages.title: Make it yours
stages.summary: Name the project, switch on the checks, and watch them pass.

steps.title: Name your project
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: The starter code is called `app`. Renaming it once, before you write anything, keeps the name the same in code, tests and docs.

do.text: Use lowercase letters, digits and dashes. It renames `src/app`, updates `pyproject.toml`, the README and CLAUDE.md, and re-locks the dependencies.

check.text: `src/my_project/` exists and `git status` lists the renamed files. Leave them uncommitted for now: main takes no direct commits, so you commit them on a branch in step `ship-02`.

undo.text: Throw the rename away. This also discards every other uncommitted change, so commit anything you want to keep first.

steps.title: Install the tools and the commit checks
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: `make setup` installs the exact versions from `uv.lock` and adds a git hook, so 18 checks run every time you commit. A leaked password stops on your laptop, before it ever reaches GitHub.

do.text: In Codespaces this already ran while the codespace was built.

check.text: One line reads `pre-commit installed at .git/hooks/pre-commit`. The first time, it then sets up each check's tools, which takes a few minutes.

undo.text: Remove the hook. The checks stop running on commit, but CI still runs them.

steps.title: Run every check
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: Proves the tools work before you change anything. `make check` runs what CI runs except the network scan, so green here means green on GitHub.

check.text: Every hook says `Passed` or `Skipped`, and pytest ends with `passed`.

undo.text: Checks only read your files, but the fixers (end of file, trailing spaces, ruff) can tidy them. Review with `git diff`; drop the edits like this:

callouts.label: Network scan
callouts.text: `make scan` adds Semgrep and Trivy. They need the network and Trivy installed, so they aren't part of `make check`. CI runs them on every push.

stages.title: Ship a change safely
stages.summary: The loop you repeat for every change: branch, commit, pull request, merge.

steps.title: Work on a branch
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: `main` is the version everyone trusts. A branch lets you experiment without touching it, and the hooks refuse commits made straight on `main`.

undo.text: Go back to main and delete the branch, with any commits only it has.
undo.code: git switch main && git branch -D my-first-change

steps.title: Commit, and let the hooks check it
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: Each commit runs the checks on the files you changed. If one fails, nothing is saved: fix what it found and commit again.

do.text: Make a small change, for example a sentence in README.md. Then stage everything that changed, including the rename from `make init`, and read the list:
Only files you meant to change should be listed. Then commit:

do.code: git commit -m "Name the project and explain what it does"

check.text: Each hook prints `Passed` or `Skipped`, then git prints the new commit.

undo.text: Undo the last commit and keep your changes staged.

callouts.label: Never skip the checks
callouts.text: `git commit --no-verify` skips every hook. Don't: CI runs the same checks, so it only moves the failure somewhere public.

steps.title: Push and open a pull request
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: A pull request runs every check again on GitHub's machines and leaves a public record of what changed and why. That record is what you show in interviews.

do.text: Open the link git prints, fill in the checklist, and press Create pull request.

check.text: The pull request shows the lint, test, scan and dependency-review checks. Wait for green ticks.

undo.text: Close the pull request on GitHub, then delete the branch from the same page if you won't need it.

steps.title: Require the checks before merging
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: A ruleset on `main` makes GitHub refuse a merge until lint, test and scan are green, even from you. It's the difference between having checks and enforcing them.

do.text: Do this after your first pull request has run: GitHub only lists checks that ran recently.
Settings › Rules › Rulesets › New ruleset › New branch ruleset. Name it main, set Enforcement status to Active, and add the default branch as the target.
Tick Require a pull request before merging and Require status checks to pass, then add lint, test and scan.

check.text: The ruleset shows Active, and a pull request with a red check can't be merged.

undo.text: Settings › Rules › Rulesets › main: set Enforcement status to Disabled, or delete the ruleset.

callouts.label: Plan limit
callouts.text: On GitHub Free, rulesets are enforced on public repositories only. A private one needs a paid plan.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Creating rulesets for a repository

steps.title: Write down the decision
steps.label: INFERENCE
steps.why: Interviewers ask why, not what. A one-page decision record for each trade-off is your answer, written while you still remember the reasons.

do.text: Copy the template to the next free number:
Fill in Context, Decision, Pros, Cons and Alternatives considered, and link it from the pull request.

check.text: The record is part of the pull request, and the description links to it.

undo.text: Never delete a decision. If it changes, write a new record that marks the old one superseded.

stages.title: Publish your project page
stages.summary: Edit the page you're reading and publish it for free with GitHub Pages.

steps.title: Preview the page on your machine
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: The page loads its words from `site/project.json`, which a browser won't read from a file on disk. A small local web server fixes that.

do.text: Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser. In Codespaces, open the Ports tab and the globe next to port 8000. Press Ctrl C in the terminal to stop.

check.text: The terminal says `Serving HTTP on 127.0.0.1 port 8000`, and this page loads.

undo.text: Press Ctrl C. Nothing was changed.

steps.title: Make it about your project
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: Every word on this page lives in `site/project.json`. Change the words there; the design system and the app stay as they are.

do.text: Edit the title, hero, stages and steps in `site/project.json`. Keep the truth labels honest.

check.text: It prints `site OK`. A typo in a key, a link that isn't https, or a route to a missing step fails with the exact field named.

steps.title: Publish it with GitHub Pages
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: Pages hosts the `site/` folder for free on public repositories. The pages workflow checks the page again before every deploy.

do.text: Settings › Pages › Build and deployment › Source: GitHub Actions.
Then open the Actions tab, pick the pages workflow and press Run workflow, or push a change to `site/`.

check.text: The pages run turns green and Settings › Pages shows Your site is live at, with your address.

undo.text: Settings › Pages › the ⋯ menu next to Your site is live at › Unpublish site.

callouts.label: Off by default
callouts.text: Until Pages is set to GitHub Actions, the workflow checks the page and skips the deploy with a notice instead of failing.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Configuring a publishing source for your GitHub Pages site
GitHub Docs: Unpublishing a GitHub Pages site

stages.title: Keep it healthy
stages.summary: Dependabot proposes updates once a week; you review and merge them.

steps.title: Review your first Dependabot update
steps.label: FACT
steps.why: Every tool here is pinned to an exact version or commit. Dependabot proposes new versions only once they're 7 days old, so a bad release has time to get caught first.

do.text: Open the Pull requests tab and pick one from dependabot. Read the release notes it links, check that CI is green, then merge.

check.text: The pull request merges and CI on main stays green.

undo.text: Revert the merge commit from the pull request page, or close an open one to skip that version.

callouts.label: Security fixes
callouts.text: Security updates skip the 7-day wait. If uv refuses a brand-new fix, exempt just that package in `pyproject.toml` with `exclude-newer-package = { urllib3 = false }`, then remove it a week later.

gates.title: Every gate in this template
gates.sub: What each check catches, when it runs, and where to change it.

rows.runs: Every commit, on the staged files.
rows.catches: Passwords, tokens and private keys committed by mistake.

rows.runs: CI on every push, and `make secrets-history`.
rows.catches: A secret committed before the hooks were on, still sitting in an old commit.
Bugs and risky calls, like SQL built from strings (S608) or `shell=True` with input (S602).
Values used as the wrong kind of data, found before the code runs.
Unquoted variables and other shell traps (SC2086).
Broken or sloppy YAML, before it breaks a workflow.

rows.runs: Every commit, offline. CI adds zizmor's online checks.
rows.catches: Broken workflows, template injection, tag pins and over-broad permissions.
Code that stopped doing what it promised.

rows.runs: CI scan job, and `make scan`. Fails if no rules load.
rows.catches: Risky patterns in any language, from Semgrep's default rule set.
Libraries with known vulnerabilities, secrets in files, and insecure Docker or infrastructure settings.

rows.runs: CI on pull requests. Private repositories need GitHub Code Security.
rows.catches: A pull request that adds a library with a high-severity vulnerability.

rows.runs: Every commit that touches `site/`, and before every Pages deploy.
rows.catches: A weakened Content-Security-Policy, inline scripts, HTML sinks, edited design-system files, and broken routes or links.

rows.runs: Weekly, after a 7-day cooldown. Security updates skip the wait.
rows.catches: Pins that fall behind, including versions with known vulnerabilities.

rows.runs: Every Claude Code session in this repository.
rows.catches: An AI helper reading `.env` or keys, force-pushing, or running infrastructure commands.

reference.title: Reference
reference.sub: What the labels mean, cards to test yourself, the glossary, exact versions, and where everything lives.

flashcards.q: What does a pre-commit hook do?
flashcards.a: It runs checks on your machine before git saves a commit. If one fails, the commit doesn't happen.

flashcards.q: A hook failed. Should you commit with --no-verify?
flashcards.a: No. It skips every check, and CI runs them again anyway, so the failure just moves somewhere public. Fix the finding instead.

flashcards.q: You pushed a token by mistake. What do you do first?
flashcards.a: Revoke it with the service that issued it, right away. Deleting it from git isn't enough: assume someone already copied it.

flashcards.q: Why pin an action to a commit SHA instead of a tag like v4?
flashcards.a: A tag can be moved to different code, as attackers did to trivy-action in March 2026. A SHA always means the exact code you reviewed.

flashcards.q: What does the 7-day cooldown protect you from?
flashcards.a: A brand-new release that turns out to be malicious or broken. Waiting a week gives everyone else time to catch it.
Static analysis: reading code for security bugs without running it. Semgrep and ruff's S rules do it here.

flashcards.q: Which check stops a pull request that adds a library with a known high-severity flaw?
flashcards.a: dependency-review, on pull requests. Trivy also flags it in the scan job.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between make check and make scan?
flashcards.a: make check runs the hooks, type checks, tests and the history scan. make scan adds Semgrep and Trivy, which need the network. CI runs both.

flashcards.q: Why can't this page run a script injected by an attacker?
flashcards.a: Its Content-Security-Policy only allows the page's own files, and Trusted Types blocks writing HTML from strings.

flashcards.q: What goes in a decision record?
flashcards.a: The context, the decision, the pros and cons, and the alternatives you turned down.

glossary.def: A project folder with its full change history, stored by git. Repo for short.
A saved snapshot of your changes, with a message saying why.
A separate line of work. Merge it into main when it's ready.
A request to merge a branch. It's where checks run and reviews happen. PR for short.
Continuous integration: GitHub runs the checks on every change, automatically.
A check that runs on your machine before git saves a commit.
A password-like string a program uses to log in. Leak it and someone else can act as you.
A named value your system hands to a program, so secrets can live outside the code.
Searching files and history for passwords and keys before they leak.
A tool that reads code for mistakes and risky patterns without running it.
Checking that values are used as the right kind of data, like text or a number, before the code runs.
Static application security testing: reading code for security bugs without running it.
A public ID for a known security flaw, like CVE-2026-33634.
Tricking a program into running attacker input as code or commands.
In GitHub Actions: pasting untrusted text, like an issue title, into a script so it runs as commands.
Breaking in through a tool or library you trust instead of your own code.
Pointing at a tool's exact commit fingerprint, so nobody can swap the code under a familiar name.
A file listing the exact version and hash of every dependency, so every install is identical.
Waiting a set time, here 7 days, before adopting any new release.
A GitHub bot that proposes dependency updates as pull requests.
A GitHub rule on a branch, such as requiring green checks before a merge.
Architecture decision record: a one-page note on a choice and its trade-offs.
A ready-made workspace definition with every tool installed, so a new machine works in minutes.
A dev container running in GitHub's cloud, opened in your browser.
A fast Python tool that installs packages and locks their exact versions.
Give each job only the access it needs, nothing more.
A list the browser enforces of what a page may load and run. Here: only its own files, plus fonts.
A browser lock that refuses to turn plain strings into HTML or code.
GitHub's free hosting for a repository's web page.
